text.title: Statistical Significance: Basics Worked Examples
text.summary: Worked numerical examples for the rules in 01-core-rules.xml. Two-proportion z-test formula and sample size calculation with a worked numerical example.

example.title: Formal H0 / H1
example.note: H0: conversion_rate_A = conversion_rate_B; H1: conversion_rate_A != conversion_rate_B (two-tailed)

list.item: 0.05 <= p < 0.10: weak evidence, collect more data
p >= 0.10: insufficient evidence to reject H0

example.title: Underpowered test
example.note: Running with 500 per variant when 57,600 are needed gives ~6% power — essentially useless for detecting a 0.5% absolute lift from 10% baseline.

example.title: Significant and economically meaningful
example.note: Conversion A=5.0%, B=5.8%, difference=+0.8%, 95% CI=[0.2%, 1.4%] — zero not in interval, significant and economically meaningful.

example.title: Worked z-test
example.code:
Inputs: n1 = 1000, x1 = 50 (A: 5.0%) n2 = 1000, x2 = 62 (B: 6.2%)
p_pooled = (50 + 62) / (1000 + 1000) = 0.056 SE = sqrt(0.056 * 0.944 * (1/1000 + 1/1000)) = 0.0103 z = (0.062 - 0.050) / 0.0103 = 1.17 p-value (two-tailed) ≈ 0.24
Result: NOT significant (p > 0.05) More data needed — difference may be real but unproven.

section.title: Sample size formula

example.title: Full and simplified formula
example.code:
Full formula: n = 2 * [(Z_alpha/2 + Z_beta)^2 * p * (1-p)] / MDE^2 Z_alpha/2 = 1.96 (95% confidence) Z_beta = 0.84 (80% power)
Simplified: n per variant ≈ 16 * p * (1-p) / MDE^2
Example: baseline=5%, MDE=10% relative (0.5% absolute) n = 16 * 0.05 * 0.95 / 0.005^2 = 30,400 per variant
example.note: Higher baseline rates and larger MDE targets both reduce required sample size. A 5% relative MDE at 1% baseline requires ~314,000 per variant; the same relative MDE at 50% baseline requires only ~3,200.
